newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major targets Labour's constitution plans.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major targets Labour's constitution plans.

text.p: Plans for a referendum on whether to change the voting system are hardly the talk of Britain's saloon bars as an election year begins.

House of Lords reform, the need for a bill of rights and plans for mini-parliaments in Edinburgh and Cardiff are regarded as similarly esoteric subjects to most Britons who look primarily at their personal finances when voting.

But as the parties prepare for the election campaign, the future shape of Britain's constitutional arrangements looks set to play almost as big a part in the debate between them as bread-and-butter economic issues.
In his first press conference of 1997, Prime Minister John Major savaged proposals by the Labour Party for the most thorough reforms to the way the country is governed since the 19th century.
"Constitutional change just for the purpose of having a so-called radical programme seems to me to be very foolhardy," he said.

Electoral reform could land Britain in the position of post-war Italy with its revolving-door governments, while a Scottish parliament with limited tax-raising powers could lead to the break-up of Britain, he argued.
Major, aides say, is convinced that despite Labour's current 20-point lead in the opinion polls, voters in the end will hesitate to back a party proposing so many leaps in the dark.
In 1992, they turned away from Labour at the last minute because of fears over how Britain would be governed.

Major believes disquiet about Labour's Scottish and Welsh devolution plans played a key role in persuading voters to give the Conservatives a fourth consecutive period in office in 1992, and similar fears can do so again.
The Conservatives accuse Labour of not daring to set out its plans in many areas of policy. But on constitutional reform at least, the charge does not stick.
Why has Labour, which used to regard the way Britain is run as of interest only to academics and fringe parties, suddenly espoused such a wide-ranging constitutional programme?
In part, it is covering its back as it moves towards the election, due by May 22, which it believes will return it to power for the first time since 1979.
The Scottish and Welsh nationalist parties have been breathing down Labour's neck in two of its heartlands, making a policy on devolution an electoral imperative.

Of the 326 hereditary peers Labour wants to prevent from sitting in the Lords, 300 are Conservatives who might frustrate its efforts to pass legislation if they retained their position in the upper House of parliament.

And a pledge to allow electors their say on voting reform provides valuable insurance if Blair needs support from the Liberal Democrats -- for whom proportional representation is the Holy Grail -- after falling short of an overall majority.
The Liberals are already involved in pre-election talks with Labour over reform plans, and recent headlines announced they have reached an accord in some of the less controversial areas.

Labour says it has concluded that the unwritten British constitution, with its reliance on precedent and its traces of a pre-democratic age, impedes the creation of the modern classless country it wants to see.

"I do not regard changing the way we are governed as an afterthought, a detailed fragment of our programme. I regard it as an essential part of new Britain, of us becoming a young, confident country again," Blair said recently.
The Conservative opposition to reform chimes with party philosophy throughout the ages that Britain's institutions should not be mended unless they are clearly broken.

"The British constitution has evolved through centuries, but it could take a matter of months for a meddling, middle-class public schoolboy (Blair) to weaken or even destroy it," Conservative legislator Graham Riddick has said.
The party is against electoral reform and Lords reform for practical reasons.
It has won overall Commons majorities at the last four general elections without ever polling as much as 45 percent of the vote, and it has a massive upper house advantage.
But it also argues against the plan to end the right of peers who inherited their titles to vote in the Lords on the grounds that it threatens the hereditary principle on which the monarchy depends.

Lord Cranborne, the Conservative leader in the Lords, has said Labour plans for reform are "ill thought-out" and hinted that his followers there could block them, creating the biggest clash between the two houses of parliament since 1910.
More practical objections lead some observers to warn all this constitution-mongering could end in tears.
They fear Labour has given so many pledges that bills on issues of greater interest to the voters could be crowded out of the legislative timetable of Blair's first government.
"After 18 years of Conservative government, haven't we got better things to do than tinker with the constitution," one left-wing legislator said.
Friends and opponents of Labour alike warn some of the proposed changes are not thought through sufficiently. The Labour leadership, they note, is split on the merits of electoral reform.

And it has no answer to a key problem posed by Scottish devolution -- that it would leave Scottish MPs voting at Westminster on English bills while English MPs would have no influence on policy in the same areas in Scotland.
